title_en: 'Contrary to What People Think, We Don't Have Infinite Money or Time' — How GTA 6 Came Together at Rockstar North
summary_en: Current Rockstar North Co-Studio Head and Head of Development Rob Nelson seems relaxed for a man in Rockstar North’s bridge, essentially moments from steering what may well be the most anticipated entertainment product launch of all time into port — after 13 long years, no less.
body_en:
Current Rockstar North Co-Studio Head and Head of Development Rob Nelson seems relaxed for a man in Rockstar North’s bridge, essentially moments from steering what may well be the most anticipated entertainment product launch of all time into port — after 13 long years, no less.
What’s perhaps more interesting, however, is how even Nelson is quite happy to concede that not even he quite knows how a game as fundamentally huge and absolutely astonishing as GTA 6 has come together so magically. Money and talent is only a part of the answer; the rest is perhaps a little more nebulous.
“I think it takes a lot of obstinance, really,” explains Nelson. “Just a sort of stubborn persistence in pursuit of the same thing for a long time, and a team that’s been together for a really long time. Now a really, really long time.
“And the answer is I don’t know. I mean, I only know my part of it, which is a part of it. And the stuff that [co-studio head] Aaron [Garbutt] does, and the stuff that [director of technology] Phil [Hooker] does, and the stuff that the programming team does, I don’t know. They just do it and we sort of build it up in layers.”
Nelson explains that Hooker sent an update through to the team very recently that showcased the progress of missions, areas, and features in the game over the last few years, and says it was “shocking to see how far it’s come.”
“Well, unfortunately, lots of people saw it in the hack that we had a few years ago — where [the game] was,” he says. “And I think in development you forget that. You forget the doldrums that you go through and you just sort of cling on to little wins every day, day by day or week by week. Sometimes they feel few and far between — certainly when you’re a few years out. And it’s just trust in the people that you’ve worked with for a long time that they’re going to hold up their end of it.”
“And this game had to rely on that. It probably sounds like a cliché answer, but this team and this game needed that more than we’ve ever had, because we’re larger than we’ve ever been — double the size that we were on RDR 2 — more spread out than we’ve ever been in terms of studios all over the world. Time zones. COVID.
“And you sit in it for week after week and just go, ‘Is this thing ever going to come together? Are we ever going to find it?’ But I think because we’ve been pursuing the same thing for a long time, every team knows what they generally want to do and want to evolve, and they just get on with it. And we work in these sort of eight-week sprints and pull a bunch of stuff together, evaluate it, make a bunch of notes, go back, iterate, iterate, iterate.”
Teams getting on with it appears to be precisely how fantastic and unexpected flourishes make their way to the final product. I note an example, which is the fact that there's now a unique animation solution for characters to get out of cars in skinny gaps, when the door can’t open all the way. Nelson lights up.
“There’s so many examples of it across the game, but that is a great example of one where the team just does their thing,” he says. “That hit a build one day and I played it just like you played it. And I was, like, ‘Holy shit, look at this. It’s amazing.’ I never asked for it. As far as I know, none of the other heads of development asked for it. The team did it. The animation directors decided that they wanted to do it.
“And that’s the most exciting thing, I think, for this team working on this stuff. It’s that there’s so many talented and experienced people working on it, and caring equally about their part, that every build is exciting. That’s I think what sustains you. It’s like every time you get a new build and there’s new stuff hitting it. It gives you energy to keep going.
“And it can be anything. It could be new ads on the radio, or just the radio going live for the first time. It can be new UI elements coming in to try, or little touches like that and you go, ‘Okay, all right, we’re just going to keep going.’ But, yeah, that’s a great example of something that just the team did off their own back.”
Nelson concedes that this approach does have to be managed, because without any guardrails, “every team will go crazy and go on forever.”
“And so there’s a bit of a contract there between all of us, including ourselves; having checks and balances in terms of where we push, how far we push, how hard we push, and how much resource [something] is worth, because everything is time and resource spent,” he says. “And contrary to what people think, we don’t have infinite money or time, or resource. So we do have to make decisions.”
On the topic of decisions, Rockstar’s confirmation that GTA 6 runs at 30 frames per second across all platforms including PS5 Pro became a popular talking point last week. Speaking with Nelson about what would have to fundamentally change about GTA 6 – and when – if the game had targeted 60fps, the Rockstar North veteran has a very simple answer.
“Too much, too much,” he says “It wouldn’t have been acceptable to anybody. The simple answer is, when you ask the technical team, they’re, like, ‘Have you seen it?’ There’s too many compromises that would’ve had to have been made to do that, is the short answer.”
In simple terms, the frame rate had to be limited somewhere in order to achieve Rockstar’s artistic vision. While the team is not ruling out things being different on future hardware, GTA 6’s sheer amount of visual fidelity, the complexity of its simulation, and the amount of systems and gameplay options it has would simply not be possible on current hardware at higher frame rate.
After playing it for the last three weeks I can’t imagine removing anything. Interestingly, it appears Nelson plays GTA 6 in an extremely similar way to the style of play I settled into during the review period – particularly in the way he prepares prior to open-world store and bank heists.
“I love just going into a store and buying a six-pack and walking down the street, drinking them one at a time, getting progressively more belligerent ’til I’m throwing the last two and talking to people,” grins Nelson. “And then I’ll call Lucia and see if she wants to hang out and sort of walk around”
“Just watching the world, the city, pass from day to night and seeing the population change and seeing people out for a night out. I think it’s that. I think it’s the fact that you can really feel like you’re embodying your version of these characters in that world. And then you could go from playing that solo to being on a date and walking around holding hands, and you can stroll down the beach or go into a nightclub and dance together, or go robbing together.”
As I discovered myself over the last few weeks, Nelson explains that the amount of preparation you want to do typically determines how successful your crime spree will be.
“I like to get just all of it ready,” he says. “I’ll just get a big vehicle, a big truck that I’ve souped up that can hold six bags, and I’ll park it somewhere close by. Then I’ll go steal a motorcycle that I don’t own and park it really close to where I’m going to go rob, go in and rob it, come out, take off on the motorcycle, stash the bags in the truck, go hit some more, [and] load the truck up with bags. Then you could either send your partner to go fence it, or go fence them yourself.”

Luke Reilly is an award-winning journalist with 23 years of media experience. He previously served as Editor of Official PlayStation Magazine – Australia and Australian 360, before joining IGN in 2011. You can find him on Bluesky @mrlukereilly to ask him things about stuff.
